children: By Carol Ryan
If the products at Louis Vuitton and Prada were suddenly 30% cheaper than Zara or H&M, it wouldn't take long for shoppers to strip the luxury brands' shelves bare.

An investing equivalent is happening in the stock market, where shares in Louis Vuitton's owner, LVMH, and Prada are trading at an unusually big discount to the two fast-fashion companies. The fact that investors aren't pouncing reflects a growing fear that some luxury brands' best days are behind them.

Global luxury sales have barely grown in three years. The debate in the sector is whether this is a temporary blip or something more serious. Two trends that made luxury stocks an amazing investment over the past 20 years-booming Chinese demand and growing ranks of middle-class consumers splurging on luxury goods in the West-are fading. This means the industry's old 8% annual growth rate won't return soon.
China's consumers were responsible for more than half of the industry's growth over the last 30 years, but they seem to be in worse shape than the country's official GDP figures suggest.

Chinese households are dipping into their savings. But this hasn't boosted retail sales, which have grown by less than 1% for five months in a row, according to research and brokerage firm Bernstein. This could be a sign that budgets are so stretched that consumers are using their savings for day-to-day living expenses.

Although home prices have stabilized in Tier 1 cities like Beijing, they are still falling in areas where 90% of the population lives, according to Bernstein. Overall real-estate values are down 40% from their peaks in late 2021 in China, representing an even worse property downturn than was seen in the U.S. after the 2008 financial crisis. Homeowners feel poorer, so they are spending less on luxury goods.

There might be more pain on the way. This summer, Beijing announced a 20% tax on offshore trusts held by citizens. A fall in sales at luxury malls in July could be an early sign that wealthy Chinese shoppers are pulling back on big-ticket spending as they expect painful tax bills. Third-quarter sales updates will show whether this is affecting luxury brands like Hermès that cater to rich shoppers.

Meanwhile, middle-income consumers in Europe and the U.S. also have less cash to spend. They face a fresh round of inflation as war with Iran pushes energy costs higher. Rising government bond yields mean consumers will pay more when they borrow to buy a new home or a car, so there will be less money left over for $4,000 handbags.

This leaves luxury brands reliant on a narrow group of ultrawealthy consumers who are still spending. For labels like Brunello Cucinelli that already sell most of their goods to the ultrarich, things will be business as usual.

But a mega brand like Louis Vuitton sells luxury to the masses. The company gets more than half its sales from middle-income shoppers who don't spend huge sums of money individually, but make up a large share of the customer base and make perhaps one big purchase a year.

This explains why investors aren't snapping up LVMH or Prada, even though their shares are cheap by historical standards. As a multiple of expected earnings, LVMH is trading at a 30% discount to Zara's owner Inditex.

The last time a discount of this size opened up was in 2016. Back then, sales growth at LVMH had slowed because consumers were tired of heavily logoed handbags and ostentatious displays of wealth became risky in China.

Louis Vuitton successfully overhauled its products and Chinese demand began to pick up again. The company also increased its focus on the U.S. after 2020. Any investor who bought LVMH's stock in early 2016 and held on to it for the next five years made total annual returns of 34%, including reinvested dividends.

The case for buying the shares today is murkier. As well as squeezed incomes, Morgan Stanley analysts point out that luxury brands face stiff competition from luxury resellers, which wasn't the case a decade ago. The RealReal's sales rose 17% in the second quarter.
The market is signaling that cheaper fashion brands like H&M and Zara could benefit as former luxury shoppers trade down to more affordable options.

Cartier owner Richemont is faring better than LVMH. Its stock is trading at the same earnings multiple as Inditex. Cartier's sales have been booming as the brand does a good job of attracting customers at different ends of the income spectrum, which might now be the key to success in a K-shaped economy. The price of its goods range from a few hundred dollars for a simple ring, to $10 million or higher for a custom necklace.

With their customers slipping financially, luxury brands face a choice to make their goods more affordable or to hold the line on prices and let their businesses shrink. Either way, luxury stocks are becoming a very different proposition to investors who used to prize them for their strong growth, high operating margins and seemingly infinite pricing power.
There is a lively debate on social media about whether luxury brands offer shoppers value for money anymore. Based on what is happening in the stock market, investors have reservations too.
